title: Forces and Newton's Laws
bigQuestion: Why do things speed up, slow down, turn or stay still, and how can we predict it?

story.title: The Egg Drop
story.kicker: One raw egg, two stories of stairwell, and a design that has to stop it gently.
paragraphs: Maya stands at the top of the school stairwell with a raw egg. It sits inside a shell she built from a paper cup, three straws and a plastic grocery bag tied at the corners like a parachute. Below her, on the tile floor, the class has taped a target. The rule is simple: drop it from the second-floor railing, and the egg must survive.

The first team goes before her. Their egg is wrapped in tape and nothing else. It falls fast, hits with a sharp crack, and yellow yolk spreads across the tile. The floor stopped that egg in a tiny fraction of a second. All of its motion had to vanish almost at once, and the shell could not take that.

Maya lets go. The bag opens, catches the air, and the whole package drifts down slower than the first egg. When it lands, the straws bend and the cup crumples. The egg inside rolls out without a crack. The class cheers, but her teacher asks the harder question: why did it work?

Maya thinks it through. The parachute pushed against the air, so the egg never got going very fast. The straws and the crumpling cup made the stop take longer, a soft squish instead of a sharp crack. A gentler stop over more time means a smaller force on the egg. That is the same idea inside a bike helmet, a car bumper and the airbag in a steering wheel.

Every force in this chapter shows up in that stairwell. Gravity pulled the egg down. Air pushed up on the bag. The floor pushed up on the cup. Each push and pull changed how the egg moved, and each one can be measured and predicted. Isaac Newton wrote down the rules in 1687, and engineers still use them to design every car, bridge and spacecraft.
story.think: The taped egg and Maya's egg both fell the same distance. What was different about how each one stopped, and why did that matter?

lessons.title: Pushes, Pulls and Net Force
lessons.mainIdea: A force is a push or a pull with a size and a direction, and only the total, or net, force changes how something moves.
reading: Push a shopping cart and it rolls. Pull a wagon and it follows you. A *force* is any push or pull on an object. Every force has a size, measured in a unit called the *newton*, and a direction. One newton is about the weight of a small apple in your hand. A gentle push might be 5 newtons. A car engine can push with thousands.

Most objects have several forces on them at the same time. A book on a desk has gravity pulling it down and the desk pushing it up. Two students can push the same box from opposite sides. To predict what happens, you add the forces up, keeping track of direction. The total is called the *net force*.

If two forces are the same size and point in opposite directions, they cancel. The net force is zero, and the motion does not change. If one is bigger, the net force points in the direction of the bigger force. In a tug of war, the rope moves toward the team with the greater pull, and the difference between the two pulls is what moves it.

Drawing forces as arrows helps. A longer arrow means a bigger force, and the arrow points in the force's direction. Engineers draw these arrow diagrams for bridges, chairs and rockets before they build anything. The question is always the same: what is the net force, and which way does it point?

words.d: a push or a pull on an object; it has a size and a direction
the unit used to measure force; about the weight of a small apple
the total of all the forces on an object after opposite directions cancel

look.title: Two Pushes on One Box
look.text: A box sits on a smooth gym floor. Ana pushes it to the right with 30 newtons. Ben pushes it to the left with 20 newtons. The box starts sliding slowly to the right. Then a third student, Cal, joins Ben and adds 10 newtons of push to the left. The box slows and stops moving in either direction, even though three people are still pushing hard.
look.prompt: What is the net force on the box after Cal joins, and why does the box stop changing its motion even though everyone is still pushing?

check.q: Two students push a box from opposite sides with exactly 40 newtons each. What is the net force on the box?
choices: 80 newtons
40 newtons
20 newtons
0 newtons
check.why: Equal forces in opposite directions cancel, so the total is zero and the box's motion does not change.

check.q: Which of these best describes a force?
choices: A push or a pull with a size and a direction
Any kind of energy stored in an object
The speed at which something moves
The weight of an object only
check.why: A force is a push or a pull. Weight is one kind of force, but pushes from hands, engines and floors are forces too.

check.q: A rope in a tug of war moves to the left. What must be true?
choices: The left team is heavier
The right team pulled harder
The left team pulled harder than the right team
Both teams pulled with equal force
check.why: The rope moves in the direction of the net force, which points toward the team pulling harder.

lessons.title: Motion Keeps Going
lessons.mainIdea: Newton's first law: with no net force, a resting object stays at rest and a moving object keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line.
reading: Slide a hockey puck across a rough rug and it stops fast. Slide it on ice and it glides far. On a perfectly smooth surface with no air, it would keep going forever. Nothing has to push it to keep it moving. This surprised people for a long time. Aristotle taught that objects needed a steady push to keep moving, and it took Galileo's ramp experiments and Newton's thinking to change that idea.

Newton's first law says an object's motion does not change unless a net force acts on it. A resting object stays put. A moving object keeps the same speed and the same direction. The tendency of objects to keep doing what they are doing is called *inertia*. The more mass an object has, the more inertia it has and the harder it is to change its motion.

You feel inertia every day. When a bus starts moving, your body wants to stay still, so you lurch backward. When the bus brakes, your body wants to keep moving, so you pitch forward. A seat belt gives the force that stops you with the car. Without it, you keep moving until the dashboard or the windshield stops you instead.

So why do things on Earth slow down? Because forces like *friction* and air resistance are always acting. Friction is a force between surfaces that rub, and it always pushes against motion. The puck on the rug did not stop by itself; friction stopped it. Remove the friction, and the first law shows itself clearly, as it does for a probe coasting through deep space.

words.d: the tendency of an object to keep its motion the same; more mass means more inertia
a force between two surfaces that rub together; it always works against motion

look.title: Newton States the First Law
look.text: In his 1687 book, the Principia, Newton wrote his first law in Latin. In an early English translation it says, roughly, that every body keeps its state of rest or of steady motion in a straight line, unless it is made to change that state by forces pressed upon it.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, 1687 (paraphrased from the 1729 English translation)
look.prompt: Newton says motion changes only when a force is 'pressed upon' the body. What force is pressed upon a rolling ball that slows to a stop on grass?

check.q: A ball rolls across a gym floor and slowly stops. What stopped it?
choices: It ran out of force
Friction between the ball and the floor
Its inertia wore off
Gravity pulled it backward
check.why: Objects do not run out of force. A force, friction, acted against the motion and slowed the ball.

check.q: A spacecraft far from any planet turns off its engine. What happens to its motion?
choices: It slows down and stops
It speeds up
It keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line
It turns around and comes back
check.why: With almost no friction or gravity there, no net force acts, so its motion stays the same. That is the first law.

check.q: A bus stops suddenly and riders lurch forward. Which idea explains this best?
choices: Inertia: their bodies keep moving until a force stops them
The bus pushes them forward
Gravity pulls them toward the front
Friction from the seat pushes them forward
check.why: The bus stops, but the riders' bodies keep moving forward until a seat belt or something else supplies a stopping force.

lessons.title: Force, Mass and Acceleration
lessons.mainIdea: Newton's second law: a net force makes an object accelerate, and the acceleration is bigger with more force and smaller with more mass.
reading: Push an empty shopping cart and it speeds up quickly. Push a full one with the same effort and it speeds up slowly. Any change in speed or direction is called *acceleration*. Speeding up, slowing down and turning are all accelerations. A net force causes acceleration, and the amount depends on two things: how big the force is and how much *mass* the object has.

Newton's second law puts it in one line: force equals mass times acceleration, or F = m × a. Double the net force on the same cart and it accelerates twice as fast. Double the mass and push with the same force, and the acceleration is cut in half. Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. It does not change when you move to the Moon, even though weight does.

The units fit together. One newton is the force that gives one kilogram an acceleration of one meter per second every second. A 1,000-kilogram car that goes from 0 to 10 meters per second in 5 seconds accelerates at 2 meters per second per second. The net force on it must be about 2,000 newtons. If the engine pushes harder than that, friction and air are eating the difference.

The second law also explains slowing down. Brakes on a bike put a backward force on the wheels, so the bike accelerates backward, which we call decelerating. A heavier bike with the same brakes takes longer to stop. That is why loaded trucks need much longer stopping distances than cars, and why highway signs warn about it.

words.d: any change in speed or direction; speeding up, slowing down and turning all count
the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms; it stays the same everywhere

look.title: Force Needed for the Same Acceleration
look.prompt: The mass goes from 1 kilogram to 10 kilograms. What happens to the force needed for the same acceleration, and what pattern do you see?

check.q: You push a 2-kilogram box and a 4-kilogram box with the same net force. Which accelerates more?
choices: The 2-kilogram box
The 4-kilogram box
They accelerate the same
Neither one moves
check.why: With the same force, less mass means more acceleration. Acceleration equals force divided by mass.

check.q: Which of these is an example of acceleration?
choices: A car turning a corner at a steady 20 miles per hour
A train moving at a constant speed on a straight track
A book resting on a shelf
A puck gliding on frictionless ice
check.why: Turning changes direction, and any change in speed or direction is acceleration. The others have no change.

check.q: A net force of 10 newtons acts on a 5-kilogram sled. What is its acceleration?
choices: 50 meters per second per second
15 meters per second per second
0.5 meters per second per second
2 meters per second per second
check.why: Acceleration equals force divided by mass: 10 divided by 5 is 2 meters per second per second.

lessons.title: Every Push Pushes Back
lessons.mainIdea: Newton's third law: forces come in pairs, so when one object pushes on another, the second pushes back equally hard in the opposite direction.
reading: Stand on a skateboard and push a wall. You roll backward. You pushed the wall, but the wall pushed you too. Newton's third law says forces always come in pairs. When object A pushes on object B, object B pushes back on object A with the same size force in the opposite direction. There is no such thing as a one-sided push.

This law confuses people, because it sounds like the two forces should cancel. They do not cancel, because they act on different objects. Your push acts on the wall. The wall's push acts on you. The wall is attached to the building, so it barely moves. You are on wheels, so you roll. Each object responds to the net force on itself.

A rocket works this way. The engine pushes hot gas downward out of the nozzle. The gas pushes the rocket upward. A swimmer pushes the water backward with her hands, and the water pushes her forward. When you walk, your foot pushes the ground backward, and the ground pushes you forward. On ice, your foot slips instead of pushing, so the ground cannot push you.

Even gravity comes in pairs. Earth pulls you down with your weight. You pull Earth up with exactly the same force. Earth has so much more mass that its acceleration toward you is far too small to notice, while your acceleration toward it is the familiar fall. Same force, very different masses, very different motions.

words.d: the two equal and opposite forces that two objects put on each other
the narrow opening at the back of a rocket engine where hot gas shoots out

look.title: Two Carts, One Spring
look.text: Two lab carts face each other on a track. A compressed spring is between them. Cart A has a mass of 1 kilogram. Cart B is loaded with extra weights to 3 kilograms. A student trips the spring. The spring pushes on both carts with the same force at the same time. Cart A shoots off at a high speed. Cart B moves off the other way, but at only one third of Cart A's speed.
look.prompt: The spring pushed on both carts equally. Use the second and third laws together to explain why the carts moved at different speeds.

check.q: A swimmer pushes water backward with her hands. What pushes her forward?
choices: Her own muscles pushing on her body
The water pushing forward on her hands
Gravity pulling her along the pool
The air above the water
check.why: Forces come in pairs. She pushes the water backward, and the water pushes her forward with an equal force.

check.q: Why do the two forces in a force pair not cancel each other out?
choices: Because one is always bigger
Because they happen at different times
Because they act on two different objects
Because friction removes one of them
check.why: Each force acts on a different object, so each object feels only one of them. Forces cancel only when they act on the same object.

check.q: A rocket engine pushes hot gas downward. According to the third law, what happens?
choices: The gas pushes the rocket upward
The gas pulls the rocket downward
The rocket stays still until the air pushes it
The gas cancels the rocket's weight
check.why: The rocket pushes the gas down, so the gas pushes the rocket up with an equal force. That push lifts the rocket.

lessons.title: Why a Sudden Stop Hurts
lessons.mainIdea: Stopping a moving object takes force, and the faster it stops, the bigger the force must be.
reading: Catch a fast baseball with a stiff, straight arm and it stings. Catch it while letting your hand move back with the ball, and it does not. The ball loses the same motion either way. The difference is time. When the stop takes longer, the force can be smaller. When the stop is almost instant, the force must be huge.

The second law explains why. To stop an object, you must give it an acceleration backward. A quick stop is a big acceleration, and a big acceleration needs a big force. A slow stop is a small acceleration, so it needs only a small force. Engineers say the *impact* force depends on how long the *collision* lasts.

Think about the two eggs from the story. The taped egg hit hard tile and stopped in about a thousandth of a second. Maya's egg stopped over a much longer time as the straws bent and the cup crumpled. Both eggs lost all their downward motion, but the force on Maya's egg was far smaller, so its shell held.

The same thinking is everywhere. You bend your knees when you jump down from a step. Gymnasts land on thick mats. A car's front end is built to fold. In every case the goal is the same. Make the stop take longer, so the force stays small enough to be safe.

words.d: an event where two objects hit each other and push on each other for a short time
the moment and force of one object hitting another

look.title: The Same Jump, Two Landings
look.text: A gymnast jumps off a box onto a hard wooden floor and lands with straight, stiff legs. The stop is fast and jarring, and her knees ache. She jumps off the same box again, but this time she lands on a thick foam mat and lets her knees bend deeply. She sinks into the mat over a longer time and feels almost nothing. In both jumps she was moving at the same speed when her feet first touched down.
look.prompt: Both landings brought the gymnast to a stop from the same speed. Explain, using force and time, why the second landing felt so much gentler.

check.q: Why does a gymnast land on a thick foam mat instead of a bare floor?
choices: The mat makes her stop take longer, so the force is smaller
The mat makes her fall more slowly through the air
The mat removes her inertia
The mat cancels gravity while she lands
check.why: The mat stretches out the stopping time. A longer stop means a smaller acceleration and a smaller force on her body.

check.q: Two identical eggs fall from the same height. Egg A stops in 0.001 seconds on tile. Egg B stops in 0.1 seconds in foam. Which egg feels the bigger force?
choices: Egg B, because foam pushes harder
Both feel the same force
Egg A, because it stops in less time
Neither feels any force
check.why: Both lose the same motion, but Egg A does it in far less time. A faster stop needs a much bigger force.

check.q: You catch a hard-thrown ball. What should you do to reduce the sting?
choices: Hold your hand perfectly still
Push your hand toward the ball
Close your eyes
Let your hand move back with the ball as you catch it
check.why: Moving your hand back makes the stop take longer, which lowers the force on your hand.

lessons.title: Helmets, Belts and Crumple Zones
lessons.mainIdea: Safety gear is designed to make a collision last longer and spread the force out, so the force on any one part of the body is smaller.
reading: A bike helmet looks like a hard shell, but the important part is the foam inside. In a crash, the foam crushes. Crushing takes time, and that time is the whole point. The head stops over a longer stretch instead of all at once, so the force on the skull and brain is much smaller. A helmet that has crushed once has done its job and should be replaced.

Cars use the same idea on a bigger scale. The front and back of a modern car are built with a *crumple zone* at each end: parts designed to fold up in a crash. That folding takes time and absorbs energy. The passenger area is built stiff so it keeps its shape. The car is wrecked on purpose so the people inside are not.

A seat belt supplies the stopping force from the first law. Without it, the car stops but you keep moving until you hit the dashboard, a very fast stop. A belt starts slowing you as soon as the car slows, and it spreads the force over your hips and chest. An *airbag* inflates in a fraction of a second and gives your head a soft, longer stop.

Engineers test these designs with crash test dummies full of sensors, then change the design and test again. The numbers guide each choice. The goal is never to make the crash disappear; that is impossible. The goal is to stretch it out and spread it around so the forces stay below what a body can take.

words.d: a part of a car built to fold up in a crash so the stop takes longer
a bag that inflates very fast in a crash to give the head a softer, longer stop

look.title: The Head and the Helmet
look.text: A student drops a melon from a ladder onto concrete. It splits open. She drops a second melon of the same size from the same height, but this one is strapped inside a bike helmet. The helmet's foam liner cracks and crushes on impact, but the melon inside has only a small bruise. She notices that the crushed helmet foam does not spring back; it stays dented.
look.prompt: The foam crushed and stayed dented. Why is foam that crushes better at protecting a head than a hard shell alone that does not bend at all?

check.q: What does the foam in a bike helmet do during a crash?
choices: It makes the helmet lighter
It crushes so the head stops over a longer time
It bounces the head back safely
It stops the head instantly
check.why: Crushing foam stretches the stopping time, which lowers the force on the head. That is the helmet's main job.

check.q: Why is the front of a car designed to crumple in a crash?
choices: To make repairs cheaper
To make the car heavier
To make the stop longer and absorb energy before it reaches the passengers
To keep the engine from getting wet
check.why: The crumple zone folds up over time, so the passenger area, built stiff, stops more gently.

check.q: In a crash without a seat belt, what stops the rider's forward motion?
choices: The brakes of the car
The rider's own inertia
Nothing; the rider keeps moving forever
The dashboard or windshield, very suddenly
check.why: The rider keeps moving until something supplies a force. Without a belt, that something is the inside of the car, and the stop is fast and harmful.

lessons.title: Planning a Fair Test
lessons.mainIdea: A fair test changes only one variable at a time, keeps everything else the same, and repeats trials so the result can be trusted.
reading: Suppose you want to know whether a bigger parachute makes an egg land more gently. You could just try it once and see. But a single drop can go wrong for many reasons: a gust of air, a crooked release, a soft spot in the box. Scientists and engineers plan a *fair test* so the answer comes from the thing they changed and not from luck.

A fair test starts with one *variable*, the thing you choose to change. Here it is parachute size. Everything else must stay the same: the egg, the cup, the drop height, the floor, the way you let go. Those are the *controls*. If you changed the parachute and the drop height at the same time, you could not tell which one mattered.

Next you decide what to measure. 'Landed gently' is a feeling, not a measurement. Better choices are the time the fall takes, whether the egg cracks, or the dent left in a clay pad under the target. A phone's slow-motion video can count frames. Numbers let two people compare results and agree.

Finally, repeat. Three drops per parachute size is better than one, and five is better than three. If the big parachute wins every time, the pattern is real. If it wins once and loses twice, the parachute size may not matter as much as you thought, and that is a useful discovery too.

words.d: the one thing you change on purpose in a test to see what it does
the things you keep the same in a test so they cannot affect the result
a test that changes one variable, keeps the rest the same and repeats trials

look.title: Three Teams, Three Plans
look.text: Team 1 drops one egg from the top step with a small bag, then one from the middle step with a big bag. Team 2 drops three eggs with a small bag and three with a big bag, all from the top step, and times each fall with slow-motion video. Team 3 drops one egg with a big bag from the top step and declares that big bags always work best.
look.prompt: Which team ran a fair test? Name one thing each of the other two teams did that makes their conclusion hard to trust.

check.q: You want to test whether straw legs make an egg lander safer. Which is the best plan?
choices: Change the legs and the drop height together
Drop it once with legs and see what happens
Drop the same lander several times with legs and several times without, everything else the same
Ask other teams which design they like
check.why: A fair test changes one variable, keeps controls the same and repeats trials so the result is not luck.

check.q: In a test of parachute size, what is the variable?
choices: The drop height
The size of the parachute
The kind of egg
The floor the egg lands on
check.why: The variable is the one thing you change on purpose. Everything else, including height, egg and floor, is a control.

check.q: Why do scientists repeat a trial several times?
choices: So a single lucky or unlucky result does not fool them
Because the first trial never counts
To use up extra materials
Because one variable must be changed each time
check.why: Repeating shows whether the pattern is real or just chance. One drop can go wrong for many reasons.

lessons.title: Weight Is a Force
lessons.mainIdea: Weight is the force of gravity on an object's mass, so mass stays the same everywhere but weight changes from planet to planet.
reading: Drop a pencil. It falls. Gravity is a pull between any two objects that have mass. Earth is enormous, so its pull on you is strong enough to feel every second of your life. Your *weight* is the force of Earth's gravity pulling on your mass. Like every force, it is measured in newtons and has a direction: toward the center of Earth.

Mass and weight get mixed up, but they are different. Mass is how much matter you contain, and it does not change. Weight is a force, and it depends on where you are. Near Earth's surface, gravity pulls on every kilogram with about 9.8 newtons. A 50-kilogram student weighs about 490 newtons here. On the Moon, the pull is only about one sixth as strong, so the same student weighs about 80 newtons but still has a mass of 50 kilograms.

Gravity also gives all falling objects the same acceleration when air is not in the way: about 9.8 meters per second every second near Earth's surface. Drop a hammer and a feather in a room and the feather drifts down, because air pushes on it. In 1971, an Apollo astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather on the airless Moon. They hit the ground together.

That result matches Newton's second law. Gravity pulls harder on the hammer, but the hammer also has more mass and more inertia. The bigger force and the bigger mass balance out exactly, so the acceleration is the same. Galileo argued this in the 1600s using ramps and careful timing, long before anyone could test it in a vacuum.

words.d: the force of gravity pulling on an object; it changes from place to place
the pull between any two objects that have mass; Earth's pull holds us down

look.title: How Hard Gravity Pulls on 1 Kilogram
look.prompt: A 10-kilogram backpack has the same mass on every world. About how much would it weigh on Mars, and would it be easier or harder to lift than on Earth?

check.q: An astronaut with a mass of 70 kilograms travels to the Moon. What changes?
choices: Her mass drops to about 12 kilograms
Both her mass and weight stay the same
Her mass drops, but her weight stays the same
Her weight drops, but her mass stays 70 kilograms
check.why: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change. Weight is the pull of gravity, and the Moon pulls less.

check.q: A hammer and a feather are dropped together on the airless Moon. What happens?
choices: The hammer lands first
The feather lands first
They land at the same time
The feather floats away
check.why: Without air, gravity gives every object the same acceleration, so they fall together. Apollo astronauts showed this in 1971.

check.q: Gravity pulls harder on a bowling ball than on a marble. Why do they fall with the same acceleration?
choices: Air pushes up harder on the bowling ball
The marble has more inertia
Gravity only pulls on heavy things
The bowling ball's greater mass needs a bigger force for the same acceleration
check.why: The bigger pull on the bowling ball is exactly matched by its bigger mass, so the acceleration, force divided by mass, comes out the same.

lessons.title: Mass, Distance and Orbits
lessons.mainIdea: The pull of gravity gets stronger with more mass and weaker with more distance, and that pull is what keeps moons and planets in their orbits.
reading: Every object with mass pulls on every other object. You pull on your desk and your desk pulls on you. You never notice, because the force is tiny. Gravity only becomes obvious when at least one of the objects is huge, like a planet. Two things set the strength of the pull: the masses involved and the *distance* between them.

More mass means more pull. Jupiter has far more mass than Earth, so its surface gravity is much stronger. More distance means less pull, and the drop-off is steep. Newton worked out that if you double the distance between two objects, the pull becomes only one fourth as strong. Triple the distance, and it is one ninth. That is why astronauts far from Earth feel almost nothing.

Gravity does not only pull things down. It also bends paths. The Moon is always falling toward Earth, but it is also moving sideways fast. The sideways motion and the downward pull combine into a curved path. That path never reaches the ground. It is an *orbit*. Newton imagined a cannonball fired from a mountaintop so fast that the ground curved away beneath it. That is exactly what a satellite does.

The same law reaches from a falling apple to the planets circling the Sun. Newton's idea was bold. The force that drops an apple and the force that holds the Moon are one and the same. That single rule let astronomers predict eclipses. It helped them find new planets from the wobbles of known ones. It guides spacecraft to the Moon and Mars today.

words.d: how far apart two objects are; gravity weakens quickly as distance grows
the curved path of an object that keeps falling toward a planet or star while moving sideways

look.title: Newton's Mountain
look.text: Picture a cannon on a mountain so tall it stands above the air. Fire a ball slowly, and it falls to the ground a short way off. Fire it faster, and it lands farther away, because Earth's surface curves down and away as the ball falls. Fire it fast enough, and the ground curves away just as fast as the ball drops. The ball never lands. It circles all the way around and comes back to the mountain from behind.
look.prompt: The cannonball in orbit is still falling the whole time. What keeps it from ever hitting the ground, and what would happen if gravity suddenly switched off?

check.q: Two objects are moved so they are twice as far apart. What happens to the gravitational pull between them?
choices: It becomes one fourth as strong
It becomes half as strong
It stays the same
It becomes twice as strong
check.why: Gravity weakens with the square of the distance. Double the distance, and the pull drops to one fourth.

check.q: Why does the Moon not fall into Earth even though gravity pulls it?
choices: The Moon is too far away for gravity to reach it
The Moon's sideways motion combines with the pull to make a curved orbit
The Moon has no mass
Earth and the Moon push each other apart
check.why: The Moon is falling toward Earth, but it moves sideways fast enough that its path curves around Earth instead of hitting it.

check.q: Which change would make the pull of gravity between two objects stronger?
choices: Moving them farther apart
Making them both smaller in mass
Cooling them down
Increasing the mass of one of them
check.why: More mass means a stronger pull. Distance works the other way: more distance means less pull.

lessons.title: Electric Charge at a Distance
lessons.mainIdea: Electric forces come from charge; like charges push apart, opposite charges pull together, and the force acts without touching.
reading: Rub a balloon on your hair and hold it near the wall. It sticks. Hold it near a thin stream of water from a faucet, and the stream bends toward the balloon. Nothing is touching the water. A force is reaching across the gap. This is an *electric force*, and it comes from *charge*.

Everything is made of atoms, and atoms contain tiny particles with charge. Protons carry positive charge and electrons carry negative charge. Most objects have equal amounts and act neutral. Rubbing can move some electrons from one object to another. The balloon gains extra electrons and becomes negative. Your hair loses them and becomes positive.

Charges follow a simple rule: opposites attract, and likes repel. The negative balloon pulls on the positive hair, which is why hair stands up toward it. Two rubbed balloons push each other apart. The force is stronger when the charges are bigger and weaker when they are farther apart, much like gravity, but electric forces can push as well as pull.

Scientists describe the space around a charge as an *electric field*. It is the region where any other charge would feel a force. The field is strongest near the charge and fades with distance. You cannot see a field, but you can map it. Move a small test charge around and record the push or pull at each spot. Lightning, static shocks and the touch screen on a phone all work by electric force.

words.d: a property of matter that causes electric force; it can be positive or negative
the push or pull between charged objects; opposites attract and likes repel
the space around a charge where another charge would feel a force

look.title: The Bending Stream
look.text: A student turns the faucet on to a thin, smooth stream. She rubs a balloon on her sweater for ten seconds and slowly brings it toward the water without touching it. The stream bends toward the balloon by about a centimeter. She moves the balloon closer and the bend grows. She touches the balloon to a metal sink, brings it back, and now the stream does not bend at all.
look.prompt: Why did the stream stop bending after the balloon touched the metal sink? What must have happened to the balloon's charge?

check.q: A rubbed balloon sticks to a wall without touching anything sticky. What holds it there?
choices: Electric force between the charged balloon and the wall
Gravity pulling it sideways
Air pressure pushing it against the wall
Magnetism from the wall
check.why: The charged balloon pulls on charges in the wall. That electric attraction reaches across the gap and holds it.

check.q: Two balloons are both rubbed on the same sweater. What happens when they are brought close?
choices: They stick together
Nothing; they are neutral
They push apart
They spin around each other
check.why: Both gain the same kind of charge, and like charges repel each other.

check.q: What happens to the electric force between two charges as they move farther apart?
choices: It gets weaker
It gets stronger
It stays exactly the same
It changes from a pull to a push
check.why: Like gravity, electric force fades with distance. Farther apart means a weaker push or pull.

lessons.title: Magnets, Fields and Electromagnets
lessons.mainIdea: Magnets push and pull through space using fields, and an electric current makes a magnetic field too, which lets us build electromagnets we can switch on and off.
reading: Hold two magnets near each other and you feel them pull or push before they touch. Every magnet has two ends called *poles*, north and south. Opposite poles attract and like poles repel. The space around a magnet where these forces act is its *magnetic field*. Sprinkle iron filings on paper over a magnet, and they line up in curves that show the field's shape.

For a long time, people thought electricity and magnetism were separate. In 1820, a Danish scientist named Hans Christian Oersted noticed that a compass needle swung when he switched on an electric current in a nearby wire. Moving charge makes a magnetic field. That discovery joined two sciences into one and made the modern world possible.

Wrap a wire into a coil, run a current through it, and you have an *electromagnet*. Add an iron core, and it gets much stronger. Unlike a bar magnet, you can switch it off, and you can make it stronger with more coils or more current. Scrap yards use giant electromagnets to lift cars. Electric motors, speakers, doorbells and the drive of a Chicago 'L' train all use them.

Fields explain how forces act without touching. Earth itself is a giant magnet, and a compass needle lines up with its field. That is why a hiker in a forest preserve outside Chicago can find north with a needle that has no idea where it is. Gravity, electricity and magnetism all reach across empty space in this way: through fields.

words.d: the two ends of a magnet, north and south; opposite poles attract and like poles repel
the space around a magnet or a current where magnetic forces act
a coil of wire that becomes a magnet when current flows, and stops when it is off

look.title: A Compass Needle Moves
look.text: In a short report published in 1820, Oersted described placing a straight wire above a compass needle and connecting the wire to a battery. The moment the current flowed, the needle swung to the side. When he reversed the current, the needle swung the other way. He concluded that an electric current produces a magnetic effect in the space around the wire.
look.cite: Hans Christian Oersted, report on the effect of electric current on a magnetic needle, 1820 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Oersted's needle moved without anything touching it. What does this tell you about the space around a wire carrying current?

check.q: What did Oersted discover in 1820?
choices: That magnets attract copper
That an electric current makes a magnetic field
That Earth has no magnetic field
That compasses point south
check.why: His compass needle swung when current flowed in a nearby wire, showing that moving charge creates a magnetic field.

check.q: Which is an advantage of an electromagnet over a bar magnet?
choices: It never needs electricity
It has only one pole
It can be switched off and its strength can be changed
It is always stronger than any bar magnet
check.why: Current makes the field, so cutting the current turns the magnet off. More coils or more current make it stronger.

check.q: Iron filings sprinkled near a magnet line up in curved patterns. What do the patterns show?
choices: The heat given off by the magnet
The weight of the magnet
The electric charge on the magnet
The shape of the magnetic field around it
check.why: Each filing becomes a tiny magnet and lines up with the field, so the pattern traces the invisible field's shape.

review.q: A box is pushed with 25 newtons to the right and 25 newtons to the left. What happens to its motion?
choices: It accelerates to the right
Its motion does not change
It accelerates to the left
It spins in place
review.why: Equal and opposite forces give a net force of zero, and zero net force means no change in motion.

review.q: Which law explains why a rider lurches forward when a bus brakes?
choices: Newton's first law: inertia
Newton's third law: force pairs
The law of gravity
The rule that like charges repel
review.why: The rider's body keeps moving at the bus's old speed until a force, such as a seat belt, changes that motion.

review.q: A net force of 20 newtons acts on a 4-kilogram wagon. What is its acceleration?
choices: 80 meters per second per second
24 meters per second per second
5 meters per second per second
0.2 meters per second per second
review.why: Acceleration equals force divided by mass: 20 divided by 4 is 5 meters per second per second.

review.q: You push on a wall while wearing roller skates and roll backward. What pushed you?
choices: Your own muscles
Friction from the floor
Gravity
The wall, with a force equal to your push
review.why: Forces come in pairs. You pushed the wall, and the wall pushed back on you just as hard in the opposite direction.

review.q: Why does a crumple zone make a car crash safer for the people inside?
choices: It makes the car stop faster
It makes the stop take longer, so the force on the passengers is smaller
It keeps the car from moving at all
It makes the passengers heavier
review.why: Folding metal stretches the stopping time, and a longer stop means a smaller acceleration and a smaller force.

review.q: A student tests whether a bigger parachute slows an egg lander. What must she keep the same?
choices: The drop height, the egg and the lander design
The size of the parachute
Nothing; changing everything gives more data
Only the color of the parachute
review.why: In a fair test, only the variable changes. Everything else is a control so the result comes from the parachute size alone.

review.q: A rock has a mass of 6 kilograms on Earth. What is its mass on the Moon?
choices: 1 kilogram
36 kilograms
6 kilograms
About 60 kilograms
review.why: Mass is the amount of matter and never changes with location. Only the weight, the pull of gravity, changes.

review.q: Which statement about fields is correct?
choices: Fields only exist inside solid objects
Only magnets have fields; gravity and charge do not
A field is a kind of visible light around an object
A field is the region around an object where its force can act on other objects without touching
review.why: Gravity, electric and magnetic forces all reach across space through fields, which grow weaker with distance.
